clinicalPearls: Emerging tick-borne infection caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia that invade and lyse red blood cells; most U.S. cases are due to Babesia microti, transmitted by the deer tick Ixodes scapularis, with ~90% presenting June through August (p.1775, 1777).

Presents as a flu-like illness: gradual-onset fatigue/malaise followed within days by fever (can reach 40.9 C) with chills, night sweats, headache, myalgia, and anorexia; dark urine and jaundice raise suspicion of severe hemolytic anemia (p.1777).

Because the same I. scapularis tick co-transmits Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum, co-infection is common: about one-half of patients diagnosed with babesiosis are also infected with B. burgdorferi, so a babesiosis diagnosis should prompt evaluation for Lyme disease, and vice versa (p.1778).
Most symptomatic patients (~80%) are 50 years or older; hospitalized patients are roughly a decade older (median 68 years) (p.1777).
Splenic complications (infarction, subcapsular hematoma, rupture) can occur even with low-grade parasitemia (median ~1%) and typically affect young, healthy patients (p.1777, 1780).
harrison.pathophysiology: Babesia parasites invade and lyse red blood cells. RBC debris from hemolysis can accumulate in the renal vasculature and cause renal failure. Free hemoglobin is complexed by haptoglobin, then the oxidized heme group by hemopexin; excess free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, promoting thrombus formation and vascular inflammation. RBC lysis in splenic capillaries can trigger localized necrosis and splenic infarction; oxidatively stressed, poorly deformable RBCs are filtered and phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, and erythrophagocytosis with the immune response contributes to splenomegaly and rupture. Fever, chills, and sweats reflect a systemic inflammatory response to RBC lysis, and excessive inflammation drives end-organ (renal and pulmonary) damage. The spleen is the immunodominant organ, explaining why asplenia is a major risk factor for severe disease; protective immunity involves CD4+ Th1 cells (severe disease in AIDS and transplant recipients), and B cells/antibodies appear critical for clearance in some patients (relapsing disease after rituximab). Persistent anemia after infection clears has been attributed to autoantibodies tagging RBCs for clearance (p.1778).
additionalDifferentials: Lyme disease (concurrent or co-transmitted by the same tick)
HELLP syndrome in pregnant women at risk of tick exposure (babesiosis is an imitator)
Other causes of febrile hemolytic anemia
infectionMimics: Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum and others) - intraerythrocytic febrile illness most readily confused with babesiosis
nonInfectiousMimics: HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) in pregnancy
Other hemolytic anemias / thrombotic microangiopathies presenting with hemolysis and thrombocytopenia
additionalInvestigations: Giemsa-stained thin blood smear (microscopy) - definitive diagnosis; trophozoites appear as ring/ameboid forms, and merozoites arranged in tetrads form the pathognomonic 'Maltese cross'
Real-time PCR amplifying the parasite 18S rRNA gene (detects 1-10 parasites/uL; allows speciation; used to monitor low-grade infection and relapse risk)
Complete blood count (anemia, often severe thrombocytopenia preceding severe anemia; WBC may be low, normal, or high) and reticulocyte count
Hemolysis markers: low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, elevated total bilirubin
Liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT) and renal function (BUN, creatinine)
Indirect fluorescent antibody serology (IgM and IgG titers) - a single positive result is NOT sufficient for diagnosis because antibodies can persist for over a year
CT for suspected splenic infarction or rupture
redFlags: Severe disease especially in asplenic (congenital, functional, or post-splenectomy), elderly, and immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, transplant, malignancy, B-cell-depleting/rituximab therapy) patients
Dark urine and jaundice indicating severe hemolytic anemia, with scleral icterus on examination
Left-sided abdominal pain, unexplained hypotension with tachycardia, or hemodynamic instability suggesting splenic infarction or rupture
Acute renal failure (leading complication, ~20%) and acute respiratory failure (~7%); also DIC, shock, arrhythmia, heart failure
Parasitemia >4% (risk factor for severe, complicated disease; can reach 30-40% in immunocompromised patients)
Diagnosis delayed >7 days after symptom onset predisposes to severe complicated disease
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from massive phagocytosis of blood cells (fatal)
harrison.prognosis: With first-line atovaquone plus azithromycin, a fatal outcome is rare; of 7612 CDC-reported cases in 2011-2015, 46 (0.6%) ended in death. Older regimens (clindamycin plus quinine) had fatality rates of 5-9%. Death is more frequent in those 65 years or older. Among Medicare recipients diagnosed 2006-2013, ~1% died within 30 days; fatality was ~3% among hospitalized patients. Fatality is high in immunocompromised patients (~20%) and in those with splenic rupture or infarction (~6%). Fatigue may persist for weeks to months after treatment. Highly immunocompromised patients are at risk of persistent, relapsing infection (p.1778).
pitfalls: Misidentifying Babesia as malaria on the blood smear: distinguish by absence of central brownish hemozoin pigment, presence of extracellular merozoites, absence of gametocytes and schizonts, and the pathognomonic tetrad ('Maltese cross'); a negative BinaxNOW malaria test helps rule out falciparum malaria when microscopy is ambiguous (p.1779).
Relying on a single positive serology for diagnosis - antibodies persist for over a year after the parasite is cleared (p.1779).

Missing co-infection: failing to evaluate for Lyme disease (and other tick-borne pathogens) when babesiosis is diagnosed, or for babesiosis when Lyme symptoms worsen or fail to abate on appropriate antibiotics (p.1778).
Overlooking splenic complications, which can occur with low-grade parasitemia and in young, otherwise healthy patients (p.1777, 1780).

Routine follow-up PCR is not recommended in immunocompetent patients (parasite DNA detectable up to 3 months) since relapse is unlikely, and persistent fatigue alone does not warrant extending or resuming therapy (p.1779).
harrison.severityClassification: Severe babesiosis requires hospital admission (median stay 4 days). Severe, complicated babesiosis is defined as illness requiring ICU admission; complicated by ARDS, heart failure, or shock; or requiring dialysis, intubation, or RBC exchange. Diarrhea and nausea/vomiting are strong predictors of severe disease, and asplenia and autoimmune disorders predispose to it. Parasitemia is typically 0.1-10% in immunocompetent patients (up to 30-40% in immunocompromised); parasitemia >4% is a risk factor for severe complicated disease (p.1777-1778).
